newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon industry slams tax cut on clothing imports. [CORRECTED 15:10 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Lebanon industry slams tax cut on clothing imports. [CORRECTED 15:10 GMT]

text.p: Lebanese industrialists sharply criticised on Thursday a government decision to cut the import duty on clothes to 20 percent from 30 percent.

Jack Sarraf, Head of the Association of Lebanese Industrialists, told Reuters in a telephone interview: "The government is acting against the credibility of its earlier decisions to support local industry and against the principle of safeguarding our investments. This is not allowed."

The decision taken by the government of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri last week caused a storm of protest among industrialists, who held their latest meeting on Wedenesday after a cabinet decision failed to drop the decision (corrects timing of original decision to last week from Wednesday.)

"The industrialists denounced the decision to lower taxes on imported ready-to-wear clothes from 30 percent to 20 percent," the heads of industrial unions said in a statement published in Beirut newspapers.
"They regarded the decision as a dangerous precedent and ...a danger to the future of investment in Lebanese industry," the statement added.
Sarraf said industrialists had suggested to the government that a tax reduction on imported clothes be strictly applied to luxury items costing over $400.

"European clothes makers are not our competitors. We compete with producers of cheap clothes like Egypt and the Far East. Why should the government reduce taxes on their products when we have to pay high taxes to export to their markets," Sarraf said.
Some 2,000 factories operate in clothes manufacturing, making it Lebanon's most productive industrial sector, he said.
He said clothes manufacturers spent $313 million on machinery and equipment in 1996, compared with a maximum spending of $100 million per annum in previous years.

"They were driven by the conviction that the government was committed to supporting domestic industry. Mr Hariri has repeatedly said he stood behind industry and industrialists and most investors believed him," he said.

"As an investor, I take risks and I need to be assured that the government doesn't go back on its decisions under the influence of its mood. I am thinking of resigning. There seems to be no other way to deal with this government."
